utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning. Madam Registrar, could you call the case, please?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case number IT-05-88-T, the Prosecutor versus Vujadin Popovic et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, madam. All the accused are here. From the Defence teams, I note only the absence of Mr. Krgovic. The Prosecution, Mr. McCloskey. The witness is already present in the courtroom. I take it that there are no preliminaries. All right. So we may proceed. Good morning to you, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And on behalf of my colleagues on the Trial Chamber, I should like to welcome you back. I hope you had a restful weekend and that you are fresh to resume and finish your testimony. Mr. McCloskey had finished his examination-in-chief, and we had agreed that we'll start with the cross-examinations today. Who is going first? Madam Fauveau. Please introduce yourself to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My name is Natasha Fauveau-Ivanovic, and I represent Mr. Miletic.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: During your interview with the investigators of the Prosecution on the 16th of May, 1993 -- 2003, in fact, on page 4 in B/C/S you said that you were sending document to the corps. You meant the Drina Corps?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: He answered, but it may have been over --

utterances.speaker: DANKO GOJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I heard him say "yes."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The witness answered "yes."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Is it the case that all the documents that you sent, whatever the addressee, were ultimately transmitted to the Drina Corps so that the Drina Corps could forward them to their final addressee?

utterances.speaker: DANKO GOJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, mostly to the Drina Corps.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Is it the case that, in fact, you were not able to address documents directly to a brigade, for instance the Bratunac Brigade, the Main Staff of the Army?

utterances.speaker: DANKO GOJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No, I was not.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: When you would receive confirmation that a document was indeed received, would that confirmation come from the Drina Corps or from the final addressee?

utterances.speaker: DANKO GOJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we get it from the teleprinter operator from the other side.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: And when you say "from the other side," you mean the operator who was at the Drina Corps or the one who was, for instance, with the Bratunac Brigade?

utterances.speaker: DANKO GOJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I meant the telephone -- the teleprinter operator of the Drina Corps.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: When you would receive a document that you were to send, is it the case that you always had to type it on the teleprinter?

utterances.speaker: DANKO GOJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: So even if you received a document that was typewritten, you had to retype it on the teleprinter?

utterances.speaker: DANKO GOJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: After sending a document, would -- you put your signature and the date and time of sending on the document that you had just sent; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DANKO GOJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The date, signature, and the time when the other party confirms receipt.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: And this signature, the date and time, you would place it on the document that you had typed on the teleprinter; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DANKO GOJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Either that or the document that had been brought to me originally, if it was typewritten.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Could we show the witness P5D283? It is a copy of a telegram that had been shown to him during an interview with the Prosecution. Could we go to page 12, please. Is it, here, an example of one of the documents that you sent?

utterances.speaker: DANKO GOJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: And this is a document that was typewritten on a teleprinter?

utterances.speaker: DANKO GOJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Can we show the next page, please. Can we show -- can we display the top part -- yes, this is good. Is this also one of the documents you sent?

utterances.speaker: DANKO GOJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Is it one that was typed on a teleprinter?

utterances.speaker: DANKO GOJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Could we show the witness the next page. Is this also a document that you sent?

utterances.speaker: DANKO GOJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Again, typed on a teleprinter?

utterances.speaker: DANKO GOJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Is it correct that this document shows the name of the unit sending the document, the number and the date?

utterances.speaker: DANKO GOJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Is it correct that the document that you had to send, the documents that you received and then sent on, always bore the name of the unit, a number, and a date?

utterances.speaker: DANKO GOJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In most cases.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Was it a rule that such documents always had to bear a number and a date?

utterances.speaker: DANKO GOJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: The original document, for instance, the one that you have before you, did the original document have to bear a signature?

utterances.speaker: DANKO GOJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Can we show the witness 527, 116. That's his interview with the OTP, page 5 in English and page 4 in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Would counsel repeat the exhibit number?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] P2776. It's the witness's statement, and it is pages -- in fact 11, and page 4 in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Sir, can you see lines 8 and 9? When the Prosecutors asked you --

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, with your leave, I would like to read this in B/C/S because I believe the English version, in fact the English translation, is not precise enough.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: So the Prosecutor asked you: "This is just an example. A courier would bring it to you, something on a piece of paper, and that would be signed by the commander?" And your answer: "Yes, it has to be signed like this one, for example." Do you now remember having said that documents had to be signed?

utterances.speaker: DANKO GOJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I thought what I meant was that there had to be a name and surname.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Isn't it correct that you were, in fact, not authorised to send documents written in longhand that were not signed?

utterances.speaker: DANKO GOJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot remember.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Could we show the document P192. Is it correct that this document bears neither the date nor a number?

utterances.speaker: DANKO GOJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: And you don't know when this document was written?

utterances.speaker: DANKO GOJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Nor do you know when you received it? Could we show the bottom of the document, please?

utterances.speaker: DANKO GOJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Most probably, on the 13th of July, 1995, maybe half an hour before the time is indicated as transmission time, maybe. Maybe 14.10.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: This is a typewritten document, not one typed on a teleprinter?

utterances.speaker: DANKO GOJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Isn't it strange that this document that should be an original one that you received has neither a number nor a date nor a signature?

utterances.speaker: DANKO GOJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is odd, but --

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Is it correct that you have no proof that Lieutenant-Colonel Milomir Savcic wrote that document, indeed?

utterances.speaker: DANKO GOJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I have no proof.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: And you don't recall who brought this document to you?

utterances.speaker: DANKO GOJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't. I really don't.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: During an interview of the 26th April 2006, on the 17th page of the transcript, the Prosecutor said you typed and sent this document. Can you confirm that you indeed sent it?

utterances.speaker: DANKO GOJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It's my signature here, but I would be even more certain if I had that part that went to the corps. If I could compare the two, I believe I was the one who did it.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: In fact, that's what I want to know. How come that in the documents I just showed you, we have your signature on the documents typed on the teleprinter, and only on this document do we have your signature on the document that had been brought to you?

utterances.speaker: DANKO GOJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the question was always asked whether it was necessary to make a copy of the transmitted document, and in this case they must have said it was enough to sign this one. I can't remember why another copy of this text was not made on the teleprinter and then signed.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Since you have no recollection of this particular document, I suppose you don't know whether it was sent encrypted or through an open line.

utterances.speaker: DANKO GOJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Encrypted, for sure.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: And how do you know that it was sent in encrypted for?

utterances.speaker: DANKO GOJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: For the most part, all documents would be encrypted, with the exception of some ordinary telegrams speaking of the passage of UNPROFOR convoys and such.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Isn't it correct that for a document to be sent in encrypted form, it had to include a reference such as "Confidential," "Urgent," or a reference of that kind?

utterances.speaker: DANKO GOJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If the original document was marked as "Urgent," that would also have to be written when it was sent.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Can we show the witness the top of the document, the upper part. Is it correct that this document is not marked in any special way?

utterances.speaker: DANKO GOJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean such as "Urgent"? No.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Why, in this case, would you have sent it in encrypted form?

utterances.speaker: DANKO GOJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have just told you. All telegrams were encrypted, and they were sent in encrypted form.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: And who decided, because you did tell me that some telegrams were sent through an open line, who decided whether telegrams would be sent in encrypted form or through an open line?

utterances.speaker: DANKO GOJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Could we see again the bottom of the page. Sir, you said a moment ago that, in fact, documents had to bear a date, number and a signature?

utterances.speaker: DANKO GOJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: And we already established that this document does not have these things. Is it possible that what you wrote here, "Transmitted at 15.10," and that you marked on this copy, not on the teleprinter copy, is it possible that you sent this to Lieutenant-Colonel Milomir Savcic for his signature?

utterances.speaker: DANKO GOJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. This came in to me and I sent it.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: How can you be sure, since you have no recollection of this document?

utterances.speaker: DANKO GOJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because it's written that I transmitted it at 15.10.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: But it's not marked to whom.

utterances.speaker: DANKO GOJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You see, the addressee is in the upper part of the telegram. If you scroll it back, I'll show you.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Can we show the top of the page, please. This document is addressed to three persons, Commander of the Main Staff, to the Assistant Commander for Morale, Religious and Legal Affairs, and to the Commander of the Military Police Battalion of the 65th Detachment. Since in fact you would receive confirmation from the Drina Corps that the document was well transmitted, you cannot confirm that this document was received at any of these three destinations; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: DANKO GOJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot confirm that it reached the final addressees.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: We discussed the signature, the date and the time you put on documents. Isn't it true that you had to put a stamp, a rectangular stamp, on all documents sent and received?

utterances.speaker: DANKO GOJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We did not have that stamp in the brigade, so we just wrote it like this.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, with your leave. Mr. President, I have no further questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Fauveau. I have on my list the Popovic Defence team, but I think last time you indicated that you were not going to cross-examine this witness. I thank you, Mr. Zivanovic --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: -- for confirming that. I have the Beara --

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour. We have no questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay, I thank you. And I have the Drago Nikolic Defence team.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We have no questions for this witness. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. In the meantime, I also notice the absence of Mr. Bourgon today. All right. Is there re-examination, Mr. McCloskey?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: No, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Judge Kwon? Judge Prost? Judge stole? Mr. Gojkovic, there are no further questions for you, which means that you are finished with your testimony. You are free to go. On behalf of my colleagues, Judge Kwon, Judge Prost, Judge Stole and on behalf of the Tribunal, I want to thank you for coming over to give testimony, and we also wish you a safe journey back home.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Exhibits.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. I have the list of -- it's all the documents in the packet, because he made reference to them briefly in the interview, and of course included in that is the 13 July document that is the most significant. And of course the transcript of the interview.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Since we are not talking of one or two documents, but quite a list, I want to make sure that, first, that the list has been circulated, that we're talking of the same list, and that therefore you are all aware of which documents we are referring to. I have a list in my hands which has four pages, the last page being just one document. That is not being tendered. I don't think -- it is being tendered, yes, okay. All right, so I correct myself. I have now been given an updated list, which is a three-page list.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I don't know if the Court wants to see the original typewritten document. You may not have seen a document on a typewriter for a while, But we have it here if you're interested.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Does any one of the Defence teams wish to see it? None. All right. So we should be talking of the same list. Are there any objections on the part of any of the Defence teams to the admission of any of these documents? Yes, Madam Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, yes, I think that this is a document that the Prosecutor showed to the witness, and it was clearly stated, so I oppose it being tendered. And some of these documents are not on the 65 ter list. That's another ground. And they were disclosed to us a few days ago. And that is another ground for my objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Which document, which specific document are you referring to in the first part of your objection? I'm asking you because it doesn't follow from the rest of the transcript, at least the transcript of what has been said in the last few minutes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It seems that the translation was not quite correct. I do not oppose the admission of this document which was shown to the witness, because when the document was announced, then it was clearly stated that one and only one document would be used, and this is P192. I do not object to that document, but I do object to the admission of all the other documents because the Prosecutor said that only one document would be used. Of course, my cross-examination would probably have been quite different had it been announced that all these other documents would be used as well. As for the second part of my objection, there are documents on this list that were never disclosed to us and that are not on the 65 ter list.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Fauveau. Madam Fauveau, I have in my possession, at least, and all the other Judges have it, too, the first Prosecution list of exhibits intended to be used with this witness, which is dated 26th of April. I assume that that was circulated to all of you, in which case I don't understand your statement that had you known about these documents, your cross-examination would have been different. I mean, as I understood, Mr. McCloskey, these documents are inherently involved in the witness interview of the 16th May of 2006. Isn't that correct, Mr. McCloskey?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: That's correct, Mr. President, so this issue was dealt with at the 92 ter motion, as we know the policy and the practice there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Madam Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I completely agree the documents were mentioned during the interview, but we never received the B/C/S versions of the documents, except those that are on the 65 ter list and which were clearly identified. As for the list, it was given to us on the 26th of April, and it says on the list, if I recall correctly, that only one document would be used.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: In the meantime, do you wish to question further -- cross-examine further the witness, because he would still be here, and we'll keep him here and make him available for you.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I cannot cross-examine him now, because in order to do that I would need to look through all the documents one by one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You have had ample time to look through all these documents, Madam Fauveau. Yes, Mr. Josse.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: So far as P192 is concerned, we accept that bearing in mind the evidential threshold that this Chamber demands and requires, it now passes muster to be admitted into evidence; however, let me make it clear, its authenticity is still very much in dispute.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, but that is clear also from the line of interrogation -- line of questions by Madam Fauveau in that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Precisely, which we adopt.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But that is fully understood. I mean ... Yes. Any further objections? One moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Let's deal with P192 first. That seems to have been kept separately from the rest. This document is being admitted, and of course that is without prejudice to any submissions on the authenticity of same, which seems to have been indicated by at least two of the cross-examining counsel. As regards P2776, again that is admitted in conformity with our previous decision to admit this witness as a 92 ter witness. The other documents that appear on this list that have been contested by Madam Fauveau need to be admitted if we are to read intelligently and understand fully the interview of the witness to the Office of the Prosecution, which is at the basis of the 92 ter business, and they are being admitted for that purpose.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think Madam Registrar will look into the numbering process, because it will take us half a day to do that here. Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. President, given that there's a challenge to the authenticity of this document, we will be providing you evidence on the Drina Corps collection, how it was obtained. It's an interesting story. And this particular packet of materials that I've used and how it was found in that collection and -- so that will be something -- given this challenge, we will get one of our investigators along the line to testify about. And I'm informed that there -- that Victim Witness doesn't quite have the witness ready. He should -- the next one, he should be here any moment. It's just a transportation issue, if we want to take a little break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Right. In the meantime, let's deal with exhibits -- Defence exhibits. Madam Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I am not going to tender any documents, but I would like to have the list of the Prosecution of the 26th of April, as it was provided to us, be placed on the list. I'm thinking of the list of the 26th of April, where it was clearly stated that only document P192 would be used.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. So that list will be incorporated as a separate exhibit, and it will be your exhibit, Madam Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, and that would be 5D296.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, can we be updated -- do you wish to object?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Well, Mr. President, that's an internal document for the convenience. It's a working document. I don't see why this -- what relevance it is. It also puts a hampering on our business to -- our ability to do business, if documents are going to get turned into -- I mean, I don't know what it's there for. It's the document I used, but I just don't -- I mean, she's made her point. I don't see what putting our business document into the evidence helps with.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think it can be very much simplified, Mr. McCloskey. Basically, it is to support or provide this as a basis for her contention that since they were put on notice only -- that one document only will be used, the rest cannot be admitted because they were not used by you. So I would leave it at that. We can safely admit it; agreed? We can safely admit it, because it goes to support her contention, but let's hope that this will be the exception rather than the rule.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, just to -- as you know, because you've made the ruling, this is a 92 ter witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, exactly. Our ruling is based on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Right. So this whole other point should be moot, but I have no objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey, you know what our position is. The fact that we might not agree with the submission from anyone, it could be you or any of the Defence team, does not mean that we should eliminate from the records anything pertaining to that submission or to remove from the records or deny the party from inserting in the records what could provide a basis. Yes. Can we be updated, Madam Registrar or Madam Usher, on what's happening? Has the witness arrived or not? Please bear with us for a short while until we establish what the problem was and if it has been solved.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And, Mr. President, if I could be excused for a moment, maybe I can help with the problem, but I also was just going to see the witness off.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay, thank you. In the meantime, for the record, we notice the presence of Mr. Thayer in the courtroom. The witness is not here. He is going to arrive in ten minutes. Yes, we will resume at 10.00. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning to you, Mr. Bircakovic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Madam Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I just wanted to correct a mistake that I've made. I tendered a document, 5D300, not 296. What I am interested in, in that document, is on page 15, line 12.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay, thank you. So good morning to you once more, and welcome to this Tribunal. You're about to start giving evidence. Before you do so, you are required to make a solemn declaration that you will be testifying the truth. Please stand up. Madam Usher will give you the text of the solemn declaration. Read it out aloud and that will be your solemn declaration with us.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Please take a seat. All right. Mr. Thayer will go first and he will be followed by some of the members of the Defence teams. Mr. Thayer, he's all yours.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning, everyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Good morning, sir. Would you state and spell your name for the record, please?

utterances.speaker: STANOJE BIRCAKOVIC
utterances.text: Stanoje Bircakovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And would you just kindly spell your last name, please?

utterances.speaker: STANOJE BIRCAKOVIC
utterances.text: B-i-r-c-a-k-o-v-i-c.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And how old are you, sir?

utterances.speaker: STANOJE BIRCAKOVIC
utterances.text: Thirty-five.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And where were you born and raised?

utterances.speaker: STANOJE BIRCAKOVIC
utterances.text: I was born in Gornji Grbavci near Zvornik. My hometown is seven to eight kilometres away from Zvornik. That's where I grew up.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And you identify yourself as a Bosnian Serb by ethnicity; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: STANOJE BIRCAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Bosnian Serb.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And just briefly, what is your educational background, please?

utterances.speaker: STANOJE BIRCAKOVIC
utterances.text: Secondary school of electrical engineering.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, when the war broke out, what were you doing, sir?

utterances.speaker: STANOJE BIRCAKOVIC
utterances.text: I had just started to study at the university in Tuzla. I had just enrolled in the university in 1992, when the war began, and I stopped.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And what were your studies in at that time, sir?

utterances.speaker: STANOJE BIRCAKOVIC
utterances.text: It was the Chemical Engineering Faculty at the university in Tuzla.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And without going into any real specifics, sir, what kind of work do you do now?

utterances.speaker: STANOJE BIRCAKOVIC
utterances.text: I run a private business for civil engineering, and we specialise in finishing works in construction.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Sir, I'd just like to take a couple of moments and review with you your military service history. And I'll just recite to you my understanding of it, and when I'm done, if there are any corrections or additions you would like to make, please do so. Okay?

utterances.speaker: STANOJE BIRCAKOVIC
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: After you received the mobilisation call from the TO in April or May of 1992, you served in a local unit which was deployed to the frontline at Baljkovica; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: STANOJE BIRCAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: You stayed there until the summer of 1993, at which time you were sent to the Military Police Company of the Zvornik Brigade; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: STANOJE BIRCAKOVIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: You served in that company as a military police officer from the summer of 1993 through the end of the war; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: STANOJE BIRCAKOVIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, sir, I want to ask you some questions about when you were sent to two schools in July of 1995. Without asking you to recall a specific date, sir, do you recall learning that the Srebrenica enclave had fallen?

utterances.speaker: STANOJE BIRCAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. People were saying Srebrenica had fallen.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And sometime soon after that, do you recall receiving an order to go to a school?

utterances.speaker: STANOJE BIRCAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, sir, to the best of your recollection, what assignment were you performing when you received that order?

utterances.speaker: STANOJE BIRCAKOVIC
utterances.text: Securing prisoners of war.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. Let me just back up for a second. Prior to receiving that order, sir, to go to the school, what is your best recollection as to the specific task that you were performing at the time that you received the order, as best as you can recall? What were you actually doing at the time you received the order?

utterances.speaker: STANOJE BIRCAKOVIC
utterances.text: When we were leaving to do that assignment, we were lined up first and then we were told that we were going to guard prisoners of war, and an assignment of the military policemen in that job, whether the prisoner of war is Muslim or a Serb or any other ethnicities, is always the same, to guard the person and prevent that person from being lost.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. Let me just stop you right there. You just referred to being lined up and receiving the order. Prior to being lined up and prior to receiving that order, do you recall what your specific duty was at or about the time just prior to receiving the order to go guard prisoners? Do you remember what you were doing, where you were assigned, to the best of your recollection?

utterances.speaker: STANOJE BIRCAKOVIC
utterances.text: I think I had been given guard duty at the gate to the barracks.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. And when you refer to "barracks," what barracks are you referring to, sir?

utterances.speaker: STANOJE BIRCAKOVIC
utterances.text: Standard. It was our military barracks. There was only one.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. And let me just ask you one or two questions about your duty at the gate, and then we'll move on to this order that you received to go to the school. While you were on duty at the gate during this period of time shortly after the fall of Srebrenica, did you see any vehicles pass which you didn't recognise?

utterances.speaker: STANOJE BIRCAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, a PUH vehicle was passing, one that did not belong to our brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And when you say "PUH," are you referring to a particular manufacturer?

utterances.speaker: STANOJE BIRCAKOVIC
utterances.text: It's a military vehicle of local manufacture, I believe. Its name is "PUH." It's an all-terrain military vehicle that was usually used to transport officers and some other purposes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And is there some significance which you attach to the fact that it was these vehicles of this particular manufacture that were passing through the gate?

utterances.speaker: STANOJE BIRCAKOVIC
utterances.text: No, I did not attach any significance to it.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, I want to take you to this order that you began telling us about, to guard prisoners. Do you recall who gave you the order, sir?

utterances.speaker: STANOJE BIRCAKOVIC
utterances.text: I believe it was company commander Miomir Jasikovac who lined us up, familiarised us with the mission, and told us that we were going to guard prisoners of war in Orahovac.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And were you told to bring any equipment with you, sir?

utterances.speaker: STANOJE BIRCAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, of course. We were under full military gear when we were lined up, and that's when the order was given, after which we were put on a vehicle, a minivan, and driven to Orahovac.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And this minivan, sir, to which unit did this minivan belong?

utterances.speaker: STANOJE BIRCAKOVIC
utterances.text: To the Military Police Company.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And can you estimate approximately how many of your colleagues in the Military Police Company were with you on this minivan?

utterances.speaker: STANOJE BIRCAKOVIC
utterances.text: Between 10 and 15, I believe. I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Do you remember the names of any of those MPs or anything in particular about those colleagues that were with you?

utterances.speaker: STANOJE BIRCAKOVIC
utterances.text: I remember one surname, because I later socialised with that man. It was my colleague, Ivanovic. And I believe the two lawyers were there, too, Bogdanovic and Jovic. I don't remember the others.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And do you remember approximately what time of the day it was when you received this order and set out?

utterances.speaker: STANOJE BIRCAKOVIC
utterances.text: Late afternoon. I'm not sure, but it could have been 6.00 or 7.00 p.m.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And, sir, would you please describe for the Trial Chamber what you saw when you arrived at the school and what you were told was going to happen, if anything?

utterances.speaker: STANOJE BIRCAKOVIC
utterances.text: When we arrived in that minivan in Orahovac, the hall where they were supposed to be put up, those prisoners of war, was empty. Whether some troops still remained around the school, I'm not sure. Too many years have passed. When we got there, we did not do anything in particular. We waited around for the prisoners of war to start coming in.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And did they arrive at some point, sir? And if so, approximately what time of day did prisoners begin arriving?

utterances.speaker: STANOJE BIRCAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, they started arriving towards nightfall. I don't know exactly what the time was.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And can you describe how these prisoners began arriving at the school, and how were they being transported?

utterances.speaker: STANOJE BIRCAKOVIC
utterances.text: They arrived in buses.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And can you describe in what formation, if any, these buses arrived at the school?

utterances.speaker: STANOJE BIRCAKOVIC
utterances.text: They arrived in a convoy, and at the head of that column, and that's what I remember and I explained why I remembered it, was an APC, a UN APC. I probably wouldn't remember even that bit if that detail hadn't stuck in my mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And how did you know it was a UN APC, sir?

utterances.speaker: STANOJE BIRCAKOVIC
utterances.text: It was a transportation vehicle of the UN, visibly marked, and at that time such vehicles circulated frequently on our roads and they were easy to recognise.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Did you see any UN soldiers on this UN APC at this time, sir?

utterances.speaker: STANOJE BIRCAKOVIC
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Did you ever hear anyone talking later about who was actually driving that APC?

utterances.speaker: STANOJE BIRCAKOVIC
utterances.text: The stories later circulated that it was one of our soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, can you estimate for the Trial Chamber approximately how many buses you saw arrive that evening?

utterances.speaker: STANOJE BIRCAKOVIC
utterances.text: Around 15, 20 perhaps. You have to believe me if I say that I don't know anymore. Between 15 and 20.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. Please describe what happened after the buses arrived to the school.

utterances.speaker: STANOJE BIRCAKOVIC
utterances.text: The buses stopped one by one up there on the road, which is 150 to 200 metres from that hall. The prisoners started disembarking, and they were directed to the hall. And the procedure repeated itself until the last bus was empty.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Do you recall whether or not these prisoners were being escorted by any VRS soldiers, sir?

utterances.speaker: STANOJE BIRCAKOVIC
utterances.text: I don't remember. I suppose there were soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Did you see any Zvornik Brigade officers at the school during this time when you were there?

utterances.speaker: STANOJE BIRCAKOVIC
utterances.text: Apart from our company commander, Jasikovac, I cannot say with any certainty that I saw anyone else.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And can you just briefly describe these prisoners that you saw? For example, were they men, women, how were they dressed, what their age range was, please.

utterances.speaker: STANOJE BIRCAKOVIC
utterances.text: There were only men aged between 20 and 60, dressed in a variety of clothing, some wearing military uniform, others wore parts of military uniform combined with civilian clothes, and a lot of them were wearing only civilian clothes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And, sir, what did you do after the prisoners, all the prisoners, had been taken off the buses and placed inside the school?

utterances.speaker: STANOJE BIRCAKOVIC
utterances.text: A plan for securing the building was made. Some were stationed at the door, some in the corners, others at the back of the hall, and we had a rota throughout -- through the night.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Did you ever go inside the school that evening, sir?

utterances.speaker: STANOJE BIRCAKOVIC
utterances.text: At one point, yes, I did. I brought some water to the prisoners, I believe in a plastic canister.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Did you sleep that night, sir?

utterances.speaker: STANOJE BIRCAKOVIC
utterances.text: No, not for a minute.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: So please tell the Trial Chamber what happened the next morning.

utterances.speaker: STANOJE BIRCAKOVIC
utterances.text: The next morning, sometime around 8.00, our replacements arrived, 20, 30, perhaps 40 soldiers. I don't know the exact number. So we were free to go, but it was not possible for us to go to the barracks. We were told instead to stay around and to be at the ready.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Sir, these replacements, do you recall whether they were VRS soldiers, MUP, civilian police; do? Do you remember at all where they were from?

utterances.speaker: STANOJE BIRCAKOVIC
utterances.text: I only know that they were in uniform, but in my eyes they were all soldiers. At the time, everybody wore camouflage fatigues. At the time, they wore all sorts of military clothing, and to me it was just military uniform.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: So you were told to stay around and to be at the ready. What did you actually do during that day?

utterances.speaker: STANOJE BIRCAKOVIC
utterances.text: My colleagues and I took the road towards the main road between Zvornik and Tuzla. Some people slept. Others called on friends or family, if they had any around, to have a cup of coffee. But mostly we just milled around the yard.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And when you refer to milling around the yard, what yard are you referring to, sir?

utterances.speaker: STANOJE BIRCAKOVIC
utterances.text: I mean the yards of the surrounding houses. There are some houses perhaps 100 metres before the gym, and you have houses on both sides of the road. That's a settlement called Orahovac.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, sir, did you see any Zvornik Brigade officers at the school in Orahovac that day?

utterances.speaker: STANOJE BIRCAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did. My commander, Jasikovac, and at one point Mr. Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And when you say "Mr. Nikolic," to whom are you referring, sir?

utterances.speaker: STANOJE BIRCAKOVIC
utterances.text: I mean Mr. Drago Nikolic, who at the time was the security officer. I believe that was his title.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And do you recall where you saw, first of all, Mr. Jasikovac?

utterances.speaker: STANOJE BIRCAKOVIC
utterances.text: I really couldn't tell you the exact location. Somewhere in the yard outside the gym.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And do you recall where you saw Mr. Nikolic that day at the school?

utterances.speaker: STANOJE BIRCAKOVIC
utterances.text: The same yard, perhaps a bit further up closer to the road. He was standing together with someone else. I can't remember if the other person was a soldier or ...

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: May we have 65 ter number 1691 displayed on e-court, please. And I will be asking for the assistance of Madam Usher to help you mark this exhibit when it comes up, please. Sir, do you see an image before you on the screen?

utterances.speaker: STANOJE BIRCAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Can you tell the Trial Chamber what this photograph is of?

utterances.speaker: STANOJE BIRCAKOVIC
utterances.text: You can see the Orahovac gym and the school and the playground in front.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. I'm just going to ask you to mark a couple of things on this photograph, please. Would you first, please, circle the area where you saw Drago Nikolic at the school that day?

utterances.speaker: STANOJE BIRCAKOVIC
utterances.text: I think it's somewhere here.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. And would you just write the word "gym" above the building that you identify as the gym?

utterances.speaker: STANOJE BIRCAKOVIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And if you would just write "school" above the building that you identified as the school, please.

utterances.speaker: STANOJE BIRCAKOVIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And if you would, just in the upper left-hand corner, if you would just place your initials and today's date, please. Today is the 1st of May.

utterances.speaker: STANOJE BIRCAKOVIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And could he put, near the spot which he marked after your question, to identify the spot where he had allegedly saw Nikolic, could he mark -- could he write the name "Nikolic," please, on the same document.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: I thank you, sir. I think we can save it. And I see we're also at the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, we'll have a break. We'll try to gain a little bit of time. Twenty minutes instead of twenty-five minutes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Good morning again, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: You just finished marking a photograph of the location at the Orahovac School, where you say you saw Drago Nikolic. Do you recall approximately what time of the day it was when you saw him at that location at the school?

utterances.speaker: STANOJE BIRCAKOVIC
utterances.text: I cannot really say what time it was, but it was between 12.00 and 2.00 p.m.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Do you recall whether you saw Mr. Jasikovac or Mr. Nikolic anywhere else in or around the school on that day?

utterances.speaker: STANOJE BIRCAKOVIC
utterances.text: I don't recall.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Meek.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't have a transcript here. I don't know if anybody else does but I don't have one. We have the middle one, but not on either end.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Any of the other Defence teams in the same position? Yes, all right. We need to attend to that as quickly as we could, please. We don't have the problem, at least I don't have the problem. And the accused would probably not be following the transcript in English, in any case. But you have the same problem? UNIDENTIFIED SPEAKER: No problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No problem. All right. Let's wait until -- in the meantime, I'm talking in the hope the transcript will scroll up for you. I'm informed that at least you can follow the transcript on one monitor. Are we agreed that we can proceed, and in the meantime the technicians are looking into the matter. Yes. I see Mr. Bourgon doesn't agree.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Mr. President, we need to make markings for the cross-examination as it goes along, and we can't do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I understand that, I understand. So let's wait, because, I mean, this is especially a part which is relevant for the Nikolic Defence team. We have to wait. There is no point in ...

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Madam Registrar asked me to close mine, and now mine's locked up, so I have nothing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That can be easily solved. I mean, do you know how to log in again, Mr. Meek?

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: My computer is frozen. I can't get out of it to get back in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I see. But you have to log out and log in again. Mr. Bourgon, you are okay? You're the one who was most interested at this point in time. Do I take it that, Mr. Meek, Mr. Ostojic, that we can proceed now? All right. Okay, in the meantime, the technicians will still need to attend to Mr. Meek's computer. All right. Yes, go ahead. Repeat your question, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Mr. President, just to make sure the record is correct, it sounded like we may have lost the transcription from my learned friends basically from the time I resumed my direct, if -- or I suggest the most recent question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't know -- the question was: "Do you recall whether you saw Mr. Jasikovac or Mr. Nikolic anywhere else in or around the school on that day?" And he had started answering, "I don't recall," when we had Mr. Meek's intervention. But I want to make sure that at least you have in your record his previous answer. His answer: "I cannot really say what time it was, but it was between 12 and 2.00 p.m.," and that refers to when he saw Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: We have it, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So it's easy. Let's go ahead. Thank you for all your cooperation, all of you.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Sir, I apologise for the technical difficulties we're having. It's completely unrelated to yourself.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And I'll just go ahead and repeat, Mr. President, my prior question.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Sir, do you recall whether you saw Mr. Jasikovac or Mr. Nikolic anywhere else in or around the school on that day?

utterances.speaker: STANOJE BIRCAKOVIC
utterances.text: I don't recall that.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And, sir, at the Orahovac School that day, did you see any other VRS officers arrive, whether or not you knew their names or faces?

utterances.speaker: STANOJE BIRCAKOVIC
utterances.text: I didn't see any other officers.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Did you see any vehicles which you didn't recognise arrive at the school that day, sir?

utterances.speaker: STANOJE BIRCAKOVIC
utterances.text: I saw a Puch passing earlier. Earlier I explained that this is a military vehicle used to transport senior officers. I don't know who could have been inside. I didn't see that, but I did see the vehicle pass by.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And in your experience, sir, at the Zvornik Brigade, did any of the Zvornik Brigade senior officers use the Puch vehicles?

utterances.speaker: STANOJE BIRCAKOVIC
utterances.text: The vehicle that passed was not a vehicle of the Zvornik Brigade. It was from the outside.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Sir, did you see any civilians in the area of the school that day? And if so, what were they doing?

utterances.speaker: STANOJE BIRCAKOVIC
utterances.text: I didn't see any in the school area, but I saw them passing towards the school, because I said that I did see them just before the school. They were just passing. I didn't see them doing anything in particular.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, during that day, did you see what happened to the prisoners who were being held inside the gym?

utterances.speaker: STANOJE BIRCAKOVIC
utterances.text: At one point, I assume that this was after I slept - I slept a couple of hours, so that's why I'm saying that I'm not sure about the time periods - I saw in the schoolyard a truck and I saw prisoners of war being brought and boarded onto the truck.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: If I'm understanding that from what you're saying you may have been asleep when the truck first arrived, do you recall approximately what time of the day it was when you first noticed that prisoners were being loaded onto the truck?

utterances.speaker: STANOJE BIRCAKOVIC
utterances.text: I cannot remember exactly, but perhaps it was 10.00, 11.00, 11.30. I don't recall the exact time.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And do you recall approximately where you were located, sir, when you saw the prisoners being loaded onto the truck?

utterances.speaker: STANOJE BIRCAKOVIC
utterances.text: One of the yards that was about 100 metres or so away; could have been a little more or a little less than 100 metres away. It was from the -- it was at the top or upper part of the road.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, you've referred to a truck, sir. Was there more than one truck that arrived and took the prisoners away?

utterances.speaker: STANOJE BIRCAKOVIC
utterances.text: Several trucks.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And from the time that you first saw the prisoners being taken away, can you estimate for the Court approximately how long the removal of the prisoners from the school lasted that day?

utterances.speaker: STANOJE BIRCAKOVIC
utterances.text: I think that they were driven away throughout the day until it was almost dark, and then I don't know if they continued after we left. We left in the evening, so I'm not sure whether the operation of taking them away or driving them away was completed until then or if it continued after we left.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, sir, during this period of time when the prisoners were being loaded onto the trucks and taken away, did you hear anything that stays in your memory today?

utterances.speaker: STANOJE BIRCAKOVIC
utterances.text: You're probably thinking of the shooting. I assume that the question refers to that. Later, it was heard, and I mentioned this in my statement, at the time there was shooting all over, so perhaps these first shots were something that you didn't give any meaning to or connect to anything, but then later there were constant bursts of fire heard.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Sir, can you describe the shooting that you were just referring to in any more detail, in terms of the duration of the fire, the nature of the fire, how long you heard that particular type of shooting last that day?

utterances.speaker: STANOJE BIRCAKOVIC
utterances.text: I will repeat it once more. Besides the shooting that would stand out occasionally, there was firing all over the place, so it's a little bit hard to determine how long that particular shooting lasted. It was repeated throughout the day at certain time intervals. I really couldn't say what intervals, but it's something that went on for 15 to 20 minutes and then would stop. But there was also shooting all over, other than this particular shooting.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Understood, sir. With respect to this particular shooting that you were just referring to that occurred at intervals, can you tell the Trial Chamber how long that particular type of shooting lasted that day?

utterances.speaker: STANOJE BIRCAKOVIC
utterances.text: I said that at intervals you would hear this, accentuated bursts of fire, and this would happen, but I really couldn't tell you how many times this recurred throughout the day.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. Well, let me ask you this, sir: Do you recall approximately what time of the day it was when this particular type of accentuated bursts of fire stopped?

utterances.speaker: STANOJE BIRCAKOVIC
utterances.text: In the evening, at dusk we got into the minibus and went to Standard. I don't know if it stopped after that. Perhaps it stopped before that, but from this point in time it's hard to determine exactly what that was, especially if you keep in mind that there was shooting all over at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: To the best of your recollection, sir, at the time you left the school, was that particular accentuated firing still going on?

utterances.speaker: STANOJE BIRCAKOVIC
utterances.text: I cannot answer this question with a degree of certainty. Perhaps it was and perhaps it wasn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Sir, based upon the shooting you were hearing, what did you conclude was happening?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Do you have a problem again?

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honours. The transcript stopped again for the past couple of minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Then you should have alerted me straightaway when it stopped. Can you generally tell us where it stopped?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Page 34, line 5.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Then it's not --

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: My stopped at page 33, line 25, the answer: "In the evening."

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: That's page 34, line 5.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Oh, they're different; okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: It's not working again, Mr. President. We started up again and it's not working.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I want to make sure if you have anything missing. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I'm told that what's happening is not unique to our Chamber, but it's happening in other Chambers and other courtrooms as well today. So let's try to -- Mr. Meek, the last words you had on your -- could you read me the last two lines, please, of what you had in your transcript?

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. "Question: Okay. Let me ask you this, sir. Do you recall approximately what time of the day it was when this particular type of accentuated bursts of fire stopped? "Answer: In the evening." And mine stopped right there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. All right. And other Defence teams, do you all have up to here, at least? It seems to me. So I'm going to read for the record, because it will go straight into the transcript -- it's still not working? I thought someone said it's working now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No, it's only Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Ours is not working, either. We tried to reboot it, I think he said, and it wouldn't accept any more transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. I think we have to wait again for a solution. I won't proceed, especially since this is worrying one of the accused, in particular, if not two. Yes, I know that Mr. Bourgon has got his back, but unless I -- I see the green light from the other Defence teams, I would not order the proceedings to continue, which I don't hear. I'll say something just to confirm whether you -- it's okay now?

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Yes, it's working now, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Is there anyone else who's got the problem, or the same problem? Basically, that's what I'm interested in. I think we can proceed. So for the record, I'm going to read out -- did you recover the part which was lost? Okay, all right. So you have it there. You too, Mr. Bourgon? Thank you. You may proceed, Mr. Thayer, and sorry, everyone, for the interruption, but when these things happen, there is nothing you can do except wait.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Again, Witness, my apologies for the interruption. My question was: Based upon the shooting that you were hearing, what did you conclude was happening?

utterances.speaker: STANOJE BIRCAKOVIC
utterances.text: There was no specific conclusion. There was an assumption, though, when this repeated itself a few times, that there was the possibility that the prisoners were not being exchanged but that there was an execution being carried out somewhere. The assumption was there in my head, but it's something that I did not want to or wish to believe in, myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Sir, where did you go after you left the school?

utterances.speaker: STANOJE BIRCAKOVIC
utterances.text: To the barracks.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And on your way to the barracks, do you recall whether anyone mentioned an incident that had occurred on the school grounds itself that day?

utterances.speaker: STANOJE BIRCAKOVIC
utterances.text: Someone mentioned, I don't know who, that there was an incident during the day when one of the prisoners of war, probably very disturbed or upset, that's at least what was said, tried to take or grab a rifle from one of the soldiers, that they struggled for it, and that I think ultimately the prisoner was killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And just to be clear, sir, you have no personal knowledge with respect to that incident; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: STANOJE BIRCAKOVIC
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, the next day, sir, after this duty at the Orahovac School, did you hear people talking about what had happened to the prisoners who had been taken away in the trucks from the school?

utterances.speaker: STANOJE BIRCAKOVIC
utterances.text: There was talk that the prisoners were executed. It's true that it's not something that was talked about a lot. It was just maybe somebody would bring up the topic, and then it wouldn't be pursued. But there was talk that they were probably executed.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And during this talk, sir, did you ever hear who did the shooting?

utterances.speaker: STANOJE BIRCAKOVIC
utterances.text: It was just a general story. At least in my presence, nobody mentioned any names of people or names of units.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: So did you spend the night at the Standard barracks when you returned from the school, sir?

utterances.speaker: STANOJE BIRCAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, at some point after your duty at the Orahovac School, did you receive an order to go to another school?

utterances.speaker: STANOJE BIRCAKOVIC
utterances.text: We didn't receive any direct orders.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. Can you describe for the Trial Chamber, then, how it came to be that you were at another school?

utterances.speaker: STANOJE BIRCAKOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know if it was the next day or the day after. I'm not sure. Sometime around noon we were told to take our equipment and to get into the minivan and to wait. There were five or six soldiers there, perhaps. Commander Jasikovac then came, and he got into the minibus and told the driver to drive to Rocevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, sir, who told you to get your equipment and go to the minivan?

utterances.speaker: STANOJE BIRCAKOVIC
utterances.text: One of the soldiers. I don't recall who.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: So what did you do then, sir?

utterances.speaker: STANOJE BIRCAKOVIC
utterances.text: Nothing. The minivan set off. We arrived at Rocevic, in front of the school. The minibus stopped -- the minivan stopped at the beginning of the playing field, and then Jasikovac and perhaps one of the other soldiers - I'm not sure - told us to wait there, and then he went in the direction of the school, and he stayed there for an hour, perhaps. He came back later, got into the minivan. I don't know if we went to the barracks after that or went to some regular assignment of bringing in Serbian fighters who had left the lines, frontlines, without authorisation. I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. Let me just ask you a couple more questions about the time that you spent at the school in Rocevic. When you arrived there, were there VRS soldiers already at the school?

utterances.speaker: STANOJE BIRCAKOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know if there were any at the school, but what could be seen in front was that there was a certain number of soldiers in front of the school, maybe 20 or so, 30. I don't know exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And what brigade were these soldiers from, sir?

utterances.speaker: STANOJE BIRCAKOVIC
utterances.text: I assume that they were from the Zvornik Brigade, because I didn't see any vehicles from elsewhere. So let's assume that it was logical to think that.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And based on your experience and the events of that day, can you tell the Court why you were at the school, if you know?

utterances.speaker: STANOJE BIRCAKOVIC
utterances.text: I can just make an assumption that we were taken there probably with a similar task, to guard the facility and, I assume, the prisoners of war, because probably there was no need for that. We were pulled back from that place.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And, sir, during this period of time, were you aware that Muslims there Srebrenica had been placed at locations in and around Zvornik?

utterances.speaker: STANOJE BIRCAKOVIC
utterances.text: I had heard there was talk of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, during this period of time when you were at the Rocevic school, physically, where were you?

utterances.speaker: STANOJE BIRCAKOVIC
utterances.text: There is the approach to the school, access road, and I think we went to the little shop to buy cigarettes or something just to pass the time that we were waiting for the commander to come back.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And did you ever actually go up to the school, sir?

utterances.speaker: STANOJE BIRCAKOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: If we may have P02494 displayed on e-court, please. Sir, do you have an image on your screen?

utterances.speaker: STANOJE BIRCAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And I just ask you to take a couple of moments to orient yourself to it. Do you recognise what this image is, sir?

utterances.speaker: STANOJE BIRCAKOVIC
utterances.text: I recognise this. This is the main road from Zvornik to Bijeljina, and this is a by-road that passes by that school in Rocevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. I would just ask you to take the stylus that Madam Usher is handing to you, and if you would just mark with arrows and the words "Zvornik" and "Bijeljina" on that road to indicate which direction is towards Zvornik and which direction is towards Bijeljina.

utterances.speaker: STANOJE BIRCAKOVIC
utterances.text: If I orient myself well, I believe this is Bijeljina [marks] and this is Zvornik [marks]. I'm not sure, because generally speaking I never worked with maps.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. Well, that's your recollection. Can you mark where you remained during the time when you were at the school in Rocevic with an "X," please?

utterances.speaker: STANOJE BIRCAKOVIC
utterances.text: Here, I think [marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And if you can just turn that into an "X" somehow, or if we need to erase it, that would be fine.

utterances.speaker: STANOJE BIRCAKOVIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. And if you would just again put your initials perhaps at the upper left-hand corner, and today's date of May 1st.

utterances.speaker: STANOJE BIRCAKOVIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And I thank you, sir. And we can save this now, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Sir, did you ever hear what happened to the prisoners who were being held at the school in Rocevic?

utterances.speaker: STANOJE BIRCAKOVIC
utterances.text: People were saying that they had been executed.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Did you ever hear what happened to the bodies of the executed prisoners from the Orahovac School?

utterances.speaker: STANOJE BIRCAKOVIC
utterances.text: The stories that went around was that they were buried where they had been executed, and several months later somebody said that someone had come to relocate them.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Sir, I thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: I have no further questions at this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Thayer. Who is going first? Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Bircakovic.

utterances.speaker: STANOJE BIRCAKOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: My name is Stefan Bourgon, and I represent the Accused Drago Nikolic in this case. Before I begin, I would simply like to express my gratitude to you for accepting to meet us briefly before you began to testify this morning. And as I mentioned to you then, I intend to ask you some questions which relate specifically to your interview with the Prosecution. Do you recall me saying that to you?

utterances.speaker: STANOJE BIRCAKOVIC
utterances.text: I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, I had many questions to ask you, but further to your testimony now in chief with the Prosecution, I think I will be able to cut down on the number of questions and move along more quickly. Firstly, I'd like to confirm that you did have an interview with the Prosecution, and that was in April of 2006. Can you confirm that?

utterances.speaker: STANOJE BIRCAKOVIC
utterances.text: I think it was in April.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And you are aware that this interview was recorded?

utterances.speaker: STANOJE BIRCAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I was aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And do you recall that at the beginning of the interview, you were informed that you were a suspect?

utterances.speaker: STANOJE BIRCAKOVIC
utterances.text: I remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And you were also informed that you had the right to be assisted by a lawyer of your choice?

utterances.speaker: STANOJE BIRCAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And your response was quite clear, "There's no need for me to have a lawyer"?

utterances.speaker: STANOJE BIRCAKOVIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, let's move straight to the events concerning the -- Orahovac, which you testified about earlier in response to questions by the Prosecution. Now, it is my understanding that the reason you went to Orahovac was to provide security for the prisoners, meaning that you were there to ensure that they would not escape. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: STANOJE BIRCAKOVIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, it's my understanding, based on the information that is available to me, that the military policemen from the Zvornik Brigade who went to Orahovac with you to provide security, they were not involved in the killing of prisoners. Would you agree with this statement?

utterances.speaker: STANOJE BIRCAKOVIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And would I be right in saying that at the time you travelled to Orahovac initially, you had no idea that any prisoners would be killed there?

utterances.speaker: STANOJE BIRCAKOVIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: My colleague referred to your travelling in a minibus, and in your response you said the minibus belonged to the Military Police Company. Can you just describe this minibus for the Trial Chamber and whether you see a difference between a minivan and minibus, and how many passengers could fit in the one that you travelled on?

utterances.speaker: STANOJE BIRCAKOVIC
utterances.text: There is a difference between a van and what we call "minibus," "minivan." Minibus, as we call it, is a miniature bus. I don't know the exact number of seats, but perhaps 20 people can be seated, whereas a van, you know yourself, can take eight to ten passengers.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And the one that you used that night was the minibus that is normally used by the Military Police Company to gather the Serb soldiers who are away without permission; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: STANOJE BIRCAKOVIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, you've already mentioned who was in the minibus that night that you recognise, and I just have one quick question. Would you agree with me that - and that comes from your interview - that Bogdanovic and Jovic who were there, they were lawyers within the Zvornik Brigade?

utterances.speaker: STANOJE BIRCAKOVIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And would I be right in saying that the reason they were in that -- in that minibus that night is because there was almost nobody left in the headquarters, and that's why they were asked to go? Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: STANOJE BIRCAKOVIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, this might seem obvious to you, but to me it's very important. Drago Nikolic was not in that bus that night, was he?

utterances.speaker: STANOJE BIRCAKOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And when you arrived at Orahovac, would I be right in saying that it is Jasikovac who informed you that prisoners would be arriving and that they would stay there overnight?

utterances.speaker: STANOJE BIRCAKOVIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And you've already mentioned that the prisoners were not there when you arrived, and you also described that they arrived a little later by bus. Now, what I would like to ask of you is: Did the prisoners, throughout the time you were in Orahovac, was there two arrivals of prisoners or only one arrival of prisoners that you were witness of or that you are aware of?

utterances.speaker: STANOJE BIRCAKOVIC
utterances.text: Only once, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, my colleague asked you a question as to how many buses were there in that bringing the prisoners over, and you said that it could be up to 20; somewhere between 15 to 20, if I recall correctly, was your answer. Now, I understand there were a number of buses. Could that number be smaller, like maybe ten, per se? Is that a possibility?

utterances.speaker: STANOJE BIRCAKOVIC
utterances.text: It's a possibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And by the time -- during the time you were in Orahovac, I'd just like to confirm that you only saw Drago Nikolic once, and that was where he was where you showed on that sketch; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: STANOJE BIRCAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, you also responded to a question from my colleague that you spent some time sleeping that morning, and that of course this happened a long time ago. I'm just curious to know whether you can say for sure whether Drago Nikolic, when you saw him, those trucks had arrived or not.

utterances.speaker: STANOJE BIRCAKOVIC
utterances.text: I couldn't say that with any certainty.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And before your replacements arrive in the morning, the ones that you described earlier, it is Jasikovac who informed you that you would be replaced?

utterances.speaker: STANOJE BIRCAKOVIC
utterances.text: I'm not sure whether it was Jasikovac or one of the soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, in terms of these soldiers, you described how they were dressed, and to you they were all wearing military uniforms. Now, is it possible that these soldiers were not from the Zvornik Brigade?

utterances.speaker: STANOJE BIRCAKOVIC
utterances.text: It's possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: With respect to the presence of senior officers at Orahovac, you responded to questions from my colleague, but you also stated in your interview you heard that superior officers were there, but you did not see them yourself; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: STANOJE BIRCAKOVIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: But you did see that -- sorry for my pronunciation -- that Puch vehicle there?

utterances.speaker: STANOJE BIRCAKOVIC
utterances.text: Correct, I saw a vehicle pass by.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, according to information provided by prisoners who were held in the school --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment, one moment. Yes, Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Just for a point of clarification, with respect to the prior question regarding senior officers at Orahovac, just so the context is clear, that we're speaking about non-Zvornik Brigade member officers in the context of the questions during the interview. I just wanted to make sure that that's clear for the record, that that's who we're talking about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Do you agree with that, Mr. Bourgon?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I do agree, but it's really for the witness to say. So I can --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. You can put the question, basically, and I think if it's clarified, it's better.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I would just like, for the sake of clarification, that when you heard that senior or superior officers had been there in Orahovac, you did not -- we're talking about senior or superior officers who are not from Zvornik Brigade. Is that your understanding?

utterances.speaker: STANOJE BIRCAKOVIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, I'll say again my last question.
