According to information which was provided by prisoners who were held in Orahovac, information which was disclosed to us by the Prosecution, it appears that Mladic would have visited the prisoners in the school. And my question is: Is it a possibility that the Puch vehicle that you saw was the vehicle in which Mladic was driving?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Or being driven in. It's more likely.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I wouldn't rule it out. It's a possibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And, of course, you know who Mladic is?

utterances.speaker: STANOJE BIRCAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, one of the things you said in your interview is that if other senior officers from Zvornik Brigade had been there, you would have recognised them, and you did not see any; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: STANOJE BIRCAKOVIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, until you heard those shots or this firing that you describe, and you described this in detail so there's no need to get back to the firing, but until you reach a conclusion based on that firing, for you, you remain under the impression that this was an exchange; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: STANOJE BIRCAKOVIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And I would take it that you were shocked by the conclusion that you did not want to believe yourself. Would that be a fair statement?

utterances.speaker: STANOJE BIRCAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it could be.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And in response to a question by my colleague, you said that there was some discussion, back in the barracks at Standard, concerning the possibility that those prisoners were executed. But my question is: I would like you to confirm that at no point in time anyone came to you while you were in Orahovac to say, "Hey, the prisoners are being executed."

utterances.speaker: STANOJE BIRCAKOVIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, at one point in your interview, and this was not covered by my colleague, the issue of escorts for those trucks on which the prisoners were loaded was raised, and you stated that you were not aware whether any of these trucks were escorted, but that it would have been a normal practice to escort a truck on which prisoners were placed. Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: STANOJE BIRCAKOVIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And you, yourself, confirm in your interview, and I would like you to confirm again, that you never escorted any of these trucks?

utterances.speaker: STANOJE BIRCAKOVIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And at one point during your interview, the investigators ask you whether you saw Drago Nikolic accompanying trucks, and your answer was: "No." Do you stand by this answer today?

utterances.speaker: STANOJE BIRCAKOVIC
utterances.text: I stand by it.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, in the morning, when those replacements arrive, you did ask for permission to return to the command, but that permission was refused, and that's why you had to stay; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: STANOJE BIRCAKOVIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And although this is not clear from your statement, I assume that this permission was denied by Jasikovac, who is the same one who told you that you would be replaced.

utterances.speaker: STANOJE BIRCAKOVIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: According to your interview and your response earlier, you left Orahovac around evening time, before sunset. Now, did you return in the same minibus that you had arrived in?

utterances.speaker: STANOJE BIRCAKOVIC
utterances.text: I believe so.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, when you arrive at the barracks, and I'd like to know if that night or in any following days you heard that there was a dinner organised that night for some officers and others, other people, the night after the events in Orahovac. Did you ever hear any rumours about that, that night or later?

utterances.speaker: STANOJE BIRCAKOVIC
utterances.text: I hear that now for the first time.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: A few more questions on Orahovac, and then we can move to Rocevic immediately. In your interview, you said something that I'd like you to confirm, which is that when you are in Orahovac, not only you but also the others were there with you, your main preoccupation at the time was thinking about the security of your own family. Would that be a fair statement?

utterances.speaker: STANOJE BIRCAKOVIC
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And, in fact, would I be right in saying that you were afraid of those prisoners that were in the gym because of what they could do?

utterances.speaker: STANOJE BIRCAKOVIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: When you were in Orahovac, I would just like to confirm that no one brought any food to you during the time you are there.

utterances.speaker: STANOJE BIRCAKOVIC
utterances.text: Nobody brought food.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And I take it you recall in your interview talking about a coffee shop. Can you explain whereabouts is that coffee shop?

utterances.speaker: STANOJE BIRCAKOVIC
utterances.text: I don't understand the question. I don't remember mentioning a coffee shop.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I will ask you: During the day, when you were asked to stay at Orahovac and being kind of on standby, did you attend any place which looks or is a coffee shop along with other people? Or shop, maybe not coffee shop, maybe just shop.

utterances.speaker: STANOJE BIRCAKOVIC
utterances.text: There is a little shop there, and our minivan was parked outside it. But there was no coffee shop that I went to during the day. I went to have a cup of coffee in the neighbourhood. Yes, that much is true.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I'm sorry, that was my mistake. I was just trying to get where the minibus was parked during the day. Can you describe for us whereabouts is this shop?

utterances.speaker: STANOJE BIRCAKOVIC
utterances.text: 100, maybe 150 metres before you reach the yard. It is closer to the main road, Zvornik-Tuzla.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: A little later, I will show you a sketch and ask you also to make some markings, but for now I'd like to move to the time where you describe or you responded to my colleague that you believe you were on duty at the gate when the order to go to Orahovac initially came. Do you recall answering this to my colleague?

utterances.speaker: STANOJE BIRCAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, you said that you were lined up to go to Orahovac around 7.00 p.m. at night. Would that be approximately the right time?

utterances.speaker: STANOJE BIRCAKOVIC
utterances.text: Towards nightfall is all I can say. I didn't wear a watch then, and I still don't wear one today. Don't hold me to that word. I cannot give you an exact time.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, at that time you, in response to a question by my colleague, you stated that there was a vehicle, Puch, that drove by, and I would just like you to confirm that those vehicles, that this type of vehicle, they're only used by very senior officers like, I suggest to you, colonels and above. Would that be right?

utterances.speaker: STANOJE BIRCAKOVIC
utterances.text: For the most part, yes, but it wasn't always the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And just to -- for the sake of using an example, your commander -- do you know who the commander of the brigade was at the time?

utterances.speaker: STANOJE BIRCAKOVIC
utterances.text: You mean at the Zvornik Brigade?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: The Zvornik Brigade commander.

utterances.speaker: STANOJE BIRCAKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Pandurevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, he was a lieutenant-colonel, and I take it he did not drive around in a Puch.

utterances.speaker: STANOJE BIRCAKOVIC
utterances.text: No, he had his own vehicle.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Do you know, Mr. Bircakovic, who is Momir Nikolic? Is that a name that rings a bell to you?

utterances.speaker: STANOJE BIRCAKOVIC
utterances.text: The name I heard only later from the newspapers, perhaps, during the past two or three years. I didn't know of it before.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you. Then I'll move on to my next question, and then we can now address the issue in Rocevic. And, again, you did respond already to many of my questions, so I will move straight to the point that you did not see Drago Nikolic in Rocevic, did you?

utterances.speaker: STANOJE BIRCAKOVIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: In response to a question by my colleague, you stated that you assume, or the exact words were "let's assume that those soldiers providing security were from Zvornik Brigade," but you can't tell that for sure, can you?

utterances.speaker: STANOJE BIRCAKOVIC
utterances.text: I can't be sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And you've already stated that you, yourself, did not approach the school, and I'd just like to get to the point where in your interview, you say that you think that there were prisoners inside the school, but you did not see that for yourself, and there were no prisoners outside of the school. Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: STANOJE BIRCAKOVIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And then in your interview, you were also asked whether you saw any bodies lying close to the school. Is not -- the word "dead" is not there, but I just suggest to you that you did not see any dead bodies lying close to the school in Rocevic.

utterances.speaker: STANOJE BIRCAKOVIC
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And another thing that comes up in your interview, and I'd like you to confirm, that you never asked Jasikovac about the fate of these prisoners, whether before or after. You never put the question to him, "What happened to these prisoners," did you?

utterances.speaker: STANOJE BIRCAKOVIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Let's now move to another topic, which is a question that was asked of you during your interview as to whether you had seen any buses parked in front of the barracks in Standard the evening that you were asked to go to Orahovac. Your answer in your interview was you did not see any buses parked in front of the barracks. Do you stand by this statement today?

utterances.speaker: STANOJE BIRCAKOVIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And would I be right in saying that to this day, have you have no idea who committed killings in Orahovac and Rocevic?

utterances.speaker: STANOJE BIRCAKOVIC
utterances.text: You would be right, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, are you aware, Mr. Bircakovic, that members from the military police from the Bratunac Brigade were recently charged for the Sarajevo War Crimes Chamber in relation to the events in Orahovac? There is a mistake. It's the Bratunac Brigade and not Zvornik Brigade.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Exactly. It -- it doesn't show up in the transcript, anyway.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Let me take the question again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You don't need to. I mean, it's clear now.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Because the question is: Are you aware that some members of the military police from Bratunac Brigade have been charged before the Sarajevo War Crimes Chamber for events in Orahovac?

utterances.speaker: STANOJE BIRCAKOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Mr. President, although the witness cannot -- is not aware of this fact, this is a document I intend to ask to be admitted in evidence, and it's a document where simply the indictment from the War Crimes Chamber in Sarajevo, whereas four members of the military police from the Bratunac Brigade have been indicted in relation to events which took place in the school for both killing and mistreating prisoners.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Just to end, Mr. Bircakovic, I would like to show you a sketch. And if I can have 3D84 on the e-court, please. If you can take a look at the sketch that will appear. First, do you recognise the area that is depicted on this sketch?

utterances.speaker: STANOJE BIRCAKOVIC
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And you've already indicated on a picture where Drago Nikolic was, where you saw him that one time on that day, but I would like you to again put an "X," with the assistance of Madam Usher, where you saw Drago Nikolic that day, so that we have an idea of the distances involved.

utterances.speaker: STANOJE BIRCAKOVIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And can you write beside that or under, "Nikolic"?

utterances.speaker: STANOJE BIRCAKOVIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And the shop that you were talking about, can we see this shop on this sketch? I'm talking about the shop where the minibus was parked that day.

utterances.speaker: STANOJE BIRCAKOVIC
utterances.text: Shall I mark it?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: If you see it, I would like you to mark it, yes.

utterances.speaker: STANOJE BIRCAKOVIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And if you can write beside "shop," or just put an "S," please, the letter "S" beside this "X."

utterances.speaker: STANOJE BIRCAKOVIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And if you can put a slash and then also put the letters "M" for "Mike" and "B" for "Bravo" to indicate minibus?

utterances.speaker: STANOJE BIRCAKOVIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And if you can just sign in the bottom corner, indicate the date, and put your initials, "S.B."

utterances.speaker: STANOJE BIRCAKOVIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And I would ask if we can save this sketch as it is marked by the witness. If I may just have ten seconds, Mr. President, to verify if I have forgotten anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I just have one last question, and this is because we have information coming from various sources that the prisoners actually arrived in Orahovac sometime during the day on the 14th of July. Now, I'm not talking the date, I'm talking the day, because we have not mentioned dates so far, but that they would arrive during the day and not previously during the night. And along with the information that we have, just so that you know, we have information that comes from prisoners who were held there, information provided to the Prosecution. We have information by other military policemen, and we have a duty roster which indicates that the people you saw there along with you, Bogdanovic and Jovic, were only absent on the day.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: So I'm just asking you: Since this happened a long time ago and you could not recall the exact dates, is it a possibility that this all happened like in the day and not over two days? Just if it's a possibility, based on your memory, to the best of your recollection?

utterances.speaker: STANOJE BIRCAKOVIC
utterances.text: It's correct that a lot of time has passed since then, and what I said is what I managed to remember. That's it.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: We'll leave it at that. I thank you very much, Mr. Bircakovic, and again thank you for meeting us before your testimony, and I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Bourgon. I have on my list the -- Mr. Zivanovic, you requested 20 minutes?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: We have no questions for this witness, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Then I have the Beara Defence team that initially asked for 30 minutes and then asked for 45. Yes, Mr. Meek.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Your Honours, we have no questions of this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Nikolic is ready. I have -- Madam Fauveau requested ten minutes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No questions for this witness, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Fauveau. And then I have Mr. Haynes requested 30 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I have quite literally three questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Go ahead. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Mr. Bircakovic, I appear for Vinko Pandurevic, so that you know, and I literally have three questions for you. Would it be right that in July of 1995, you would have been able to recognise any of the assistant commanders of the Zvornik Brigade by sight?

utterances.speaker: STANOJE BIRCAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Including the assistant commander for logistics, Sreten Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: STANOJE BIRCAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: So can we take it from your evidence that you did not see Sreten Milosevic at Orahovac?

utterances.speaker: STANOJE BIRCAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Can we move on now to Rocevic? When you first arrived at Rocevic, were there already other personnel in military uniforms there?

utterances.speaker: STANOJE BIRCAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Can you estimate how many?

utterances.speaker: STANOJE BIRCAKOVIC
utterances.text: I think that I already answered this question, put to me by the Prosecutor, so it's about 20 or 30. I don't know the exact number.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: So the sort of number that might have got there in, say, one minibus?

utterances.speaker: STANOJE BIRCAKOVIC
utterances.text: As I said, I don't know the exact number. And from this time distance, it's hard to make an estimate about how many people could fit into a minibus.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Well, just one more thing. In your experience of being bussed to assignments as a military policeman, is it always the case that the bus remains while you are there or does the bus sometimes drop you off and come back and pick you up?

utterances.speaker: STANOJE BIRCAKOVIC
utterances.text: It depends on the assignment in question and what the assessment of the commander is when he sends us out on an assignment. Sometimes the minibus would drop us off and pick us up, because sometimes there are assignments in the field that take two or three days, so then it was normal for the minibus not to wait for us. Sometimes it would wait for us and sometimes it would come back for us. There was no rule. It depended on the assessment of the commander when he was sending out the vehicle.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you very much. And just one last thing. When you referred to conversations that took place after the event about the possibility that the prisoners had been executed, were they conversations that you had with fellow military policemen?

utterances.speaker: STANOJE BIRCAKOVIC
utterances.text: Not just the military police officers, but other soldiers too. It depends when you sat with whom. There would be talk.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Bircakovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Haynes. Could I have confirmation from the Borovcanin and Gvero Defence teams, respectively, that you don't have any cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: By all means, Your Honour, we stand by our position. We will not cross-examine this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. And Mr. Josse?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Confirmed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you have a re-examination, Mr. Thayer?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: No, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Judge Kwon?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, go ahead. Questioned by the Court:

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I have some questions, Mr. Bircakovic. I refrain from asking questions, but I'm tempted and I'll do it. I'll ask some questions, in particular in relation to the question: Who did the killing? To the question put by Mr. Thayer from the Prosecution, I'm at page 37, line 20: "During the talk you had with your colleagues, did you ever hear who did the shooting?" Your answer: "It was just a general story." Can you tell me what general story it was that you heard at the time?

utterances.speaker: STANOJE BIRCAKOVIC
utterances.text: I can tell you there was talk. It wasn't really much talk, that there was an execution there, that this happened, and no one, and I assume the people who talked about it also didn't know who were the protagonists in that, so there were no names of those responsible or the units. I can say that in my presence, I never heard from anyone anyone's name or the name of any unit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: During the examination-in-chief, at one time you said that, referring to the killings, or the assumption, you said that it was something you did not want or wish to believe in, yourself. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: STANOJE BIRCAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Moreover, there might have been a danger on your part that you may have been viewed to be part of those who did the killing, so if I were you, I had ample reason to find out who had done that killing; would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: STANOJE BIRCAKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, look, the events happened in the way that they happened; what anyone can say, they will go ahead and say it. Anyway, a person, particularly at that time, to try to inquire about those matters at that time was something that was not a recommended course of action.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Some people may have difficulty following your answer, that you cannot -- you are not in the position to tell who did that. One may view that you are not telling everything you know. What would you say to that?

utterances.speaker: STANOJE BIRCAKOVIC
utterances.text: I said all I know. It's a little bit difficult to understand, I assume, not going into a deeper analysis. It's a little bit difficult to understand those times without having gone through those times.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: At one time during the course of cross-examination, that you said that you asked for permission to return to the barracks. Can I ask what the reason was why you wanted to return to the barracks?

utterances.speaker: STANOJE BIRCAKOVIC
utterances.text: There was a request to return to the barracks because rest was essential after a sleepless night, so that was the reason we requested to go back and to rest.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So the request was not made by only you; the request was made by you and your colleagues?

utterances.speaker: STANOJE BIRCAKOVIC
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Bircakovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Judge Prost? Judge Stole? I just have one question. You were asked on cross-examination by Mr. Bourgon about the Puch and also about Mladic. Did you hear any rumours, at least, that Mladic was present at Orahovac at any time during the relevant period? Did anyone mention to you, "Mladic came here, was here"?

utterances.speaker: STANOJE BIRCAKOVIC
utterances.text: Nobody ever told me. I heard this information perhaps two or three years later after the war was over, in passing from a man, something to the effect that Mladic was in Orahovac. That's all I know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. So that means that your testimony has come to an end, which also means that you are free to go. Our staff will assist you and help you return home at the earliest. On behalf of the Trial Chamber, I wish to thank you for having come over, and I also, on behalf of everyone here, wish you a safe journey back home.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Exhibits. Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Mr. President, we have four exhibits we wish to tender.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: I stand corrected. We have two. The PIC 0095, which is the marked version of P061691 marked by the witness today. The second one is PIC 00096, which is a marked version of P02494 marked by the witness today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Any objections? No objections. These two documents are being admitted as exhibits, and the Prosecution exhibits will be marked accordingly. Defence? Mr. Bourgon?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Two exhibits, Mr. President. The first one is 3DIC97, which is the marked version of 3D84. And the second one is the indictment from the Sarajevo War Crimes Chamber which will soon be in court. The number will be 3D133, and as soon as it's in e-court, we have it in both B/C/S and in English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Objections?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Your Honour, this is one of those rare times that I will object to a Defence exhibit, namely the indictment that has been offered here. This witness testified he had no knowledge as to the information that was contained in my learned friend's question, and at this point I don't see any relevance to this charging document from the Sarajevo Court. If there is another witness who has a better basis of knowledge or if there can be some further relevance shown, then at that point certainly I may not have the objection I have now. But given the circumstances, I would object to this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Bourgon? Thank you, Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I would say, of course, this document is highly relevant. The fact that we have members from the military police from a different brigade who are charged for events that took place the same day in Orahovac is highly relevant. Now, whether we introduce this document through this witness or through another witness, that's a different question. The idea, this is an official document, it exists in the records of the Sarajevo War Crimes Chamber, and I don't really necessarily want to introduce it through this witness. However, it is an official document that needs to be on the record to assist the Trial Chamber in this case. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I'm going to add to this debate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Haynes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: In every book on criminal evidence I've ever read, the section under "exhibits" has, as its first section, public documents. An indictment is a public document. It proves itself. There can't be any sensible objection to this being an exhibit in this case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Meek.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours, I agree with both Mr. Haynes and Mr. Bourgon, and further I believe that the court in Sarajevo is a court of competent jurisdiction and you can take judicial notice of the indictment that's been filed publicly there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: I also want to know exactly what the OTP's position is, why they're objecting to this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Just one question, Mr. Bourgon. Is the document that you wish to tender a certified document or is it --

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Well, the copy I have is not certified, but it is a certified document, and it's a document that recently came into our possession. And we have all the stamps on the photocopies that it comes from Sarajevo. If need be, we will get a certified copy, but I believe that this is something that this Tribunal has done away for a long time, asking for certified copies. But if that be the wish of the Court, we will do so, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's just a time-honoured issue of relevance which we find in every book on criminal evidence I've ever read.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you, Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We certainly don't agree with you, Mr. Thayer, that this document would lack relevance, for the same reason that Mr. Bourgon pointed out. We acknowledge relevance there, too. The other thing is this: This witness's testimony has complete ignorance as to the existence of this indictment, so I don't know whether you will have other witnesses that will testify to the existence of this case or not, but if you do have -- of this indictment or not. If you do have, then that will solve the problem. If you don't have, I think the document would need some kind of attestation, some kind of certification. So for the time being, we are admitting it, but marking it for identification purposes until either of these two events occur or conditions occur. Okay? Yes, Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Your Honour, just for the record, we'll stipulate as to the authenticity of the document. It's simply a question of whether it's relevant to this witness or not. That's our position. We'll make it easy for everybody in that regard.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Well, if they stipulate, then we can admit it straightaway, yes? Okay. Then in that case, once there is this stipulation, we are admitting it, not just marking it for identification. Thank you. We'll have a break now, 25 minutes. Mr. McCloskey, is the next witness here? Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Your Honour, the Witness Unit is working on making sure he will be here for his testimony after the break. He is in town. He's ready to go.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So for the record, we are starting later than scheduled because, in the meantime, we were aware that there were some difficulties in tracing -- in finding the witness, who was not expected to testify today. So good morning -- or good afternoon to you, Mr. Djuric, and welcome to this Tribunal. I'm sorry we had to give you a sort of a surprise, to find you and bring you here when you were not expecting it, but we were finished with the previous witness before we had expected his testimony to end, to come to an end. You're about to start giving evidence, and our rules require that before you do so, you make a solemn declaration that you will be testifying the truth. Madam Usher is going to hand you the text of the solemn declaration. Read it out aloud, please, and that will be your solemn undertake with us.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, sir. Please make yourself comfortable, and Mr. Thayer will go first. He has a few questions for you. I don't know that we will finish today, because you asked for two hours, so I don't know that we will finish today. Certainly, we need to continue with your testimony tomorrow, for sure, if not even beyond that. Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Mr. President, I've advised the witness of this. Given his position and the circumstances in July of 1995, I think a caution would be in order.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you for that information, Mr. Thayer. Mr. Djuric, you've just heard what Mr. Thayer has said, and I would take it -- I would assume that you have already been briefed on this. There is a principle in law that a witness should not be made to answer questions which could possibly incriminate him. This is a principle that is recognised worldwide, and we usually refer to it as the right or privilege against self-incrimination. We have the same principle here, but we don't have an absolute -- you do not have an absolute right in this context. I'll try to explain to you briefly what our Rules says, and this is supposed to be a caution, an eye-opener for you, in case you are asked questions the answer to which could possibly incriminate you. So in such cases, if you are asked to make a statement, to answer a question which might tend to incriminate you, then you may object to answering that question. You need to address yourself to us, the four Judges up here. We have two options. We can either agree to exempt you from answering such questions, or we can decide not to grant you such exemption and to force you, to compel you, to answer the question or questions that are put to you. In such a case, evidence or testimony on your part which is forced, which is compelled in this way, shall not be used as evidence in any subsequent prosecution that might be taken against you for any offence, of course unless we're talking of false testimony. So did I make myself clear to you? Did you understand your legal rights? Okay, thank you. Yes, Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, sir.

utterances.speaker: MENDELJEV DJURIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And, again, thank you for coming in on such short notice. Would you please state and spell your name for the record?

utterances.speaker: MENDELJEV DJURIC
utterances.text: Mendeljev, M-e-n-d-e-l-j-e-v, surname Djuric, D-j-u-r-i-c.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And how old are you, sir?

utterances.speaker: MENDELJEV DJURIC
utterances.text: Forty-six years. I'll be 47 soon.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Where were you born and raised?

utterances.speaker: MENDELJEV DJURIC
utterances.text: I was born in Olovo, 56 kilometres from Sarajevo, and I grew up in Modrica, also in Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And you identify yourself as a Bosnian Serb; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MENDELJEV DJURIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Sir, I want to review with you your employment and service history and just ask you to confirm some of that history. If I make any errors or if you have any clarifications, please let me know. You attended the High School for Police in Sarajevo from 1975 to 1979?

utterances.speaker: MENDELJEV DJURIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: You served as a uniformed police officer from 1979 through 1982 in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: MENDELJEV DJURIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: When the Special Police Unit was created at the national level in 1982, you joined as a regular member and served with the Special Police until you retired in 1999?

utterances.speaker: MENDELJEV DJURIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: In 1988, you became a group leader?

utterances.speaker: MENDELJEV DJURIC
utterances.text: I became a commander of one group in the Special Platoon within the -- what was then a detachment.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And just briefly, sir, would you tell the Trial Chamber what your particular skills or areas of expertise were in your role with the Special Police at that time?

utterances.speaker: MENDELJEV DJURIC
utterances.text: The tasks of the Special Unit at the time were variegated. We were working on drills preventing disturbances of peace in any form, dealing with hostage situations on aircraft, on land, on water, et cetera. We had also the traditional fitness training. That would be it.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. And in connection with your service, some examples would include performing public security at the 1984 Sarajevo Olympics; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MENDELJEV DJURIC
utterances.text: Yes. One of our major assignments in that period was to prepare to perform security duties during the Olympic games in 1984 in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: You also provided security for the Sarajevo airport?

utterances.speaker: MENDELJEV DJURIC
utterances.text: Maybe not security in the real sense of the word, but since I had undergone special training for anti-sabotage, I personally had occasion to assist my colleagues from the Ministry of the Interior, dealing with entries and exits of VIPs, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And just briefly, what were some of the specialised skills which -- which you had, in terms of your training and expertise?

utterances.speaker: MENDELJEV DJURIC
utterances.text: Since every individual in that unit was the more valuable, the more skills he had, naturally we strove to acquire as many skills as possible. In addition to my specialist training from before, I became a scuba diver, a mountain guard and rescuer, I was a sharpshooter, and of course all of us exercised in martial arts. That was one of our main skills and main jobs. It was useful in many areas.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And, sir, in 1994 you were assigned to serve as a training instructor within the brigade; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MENDELJEV DJURIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And it's also the case that you completed the Higher Police School in Belgrade from 1994 through 1997?

utterances.speaker: MENDELJEV DJURIC
utterances.text: Yes. I was just taking exams in the first year of that higher school when I received a summons from the unit, saying that I should report to the unit, and the brief explanation was that we were going to Mount Jahorina.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. And we'll talk about that in just a second. I just have one last question about your background. Can you just tell the Trial Chamber, generally speaking, without any specifics, what kind of work have you been doing since your retirement in 1999?

utterances.speaker: MENDELJEV DJURIC
utterances.text: From the moment I retired, I was forced to go into business of some kind because retirement pensions are very low. My attempts at commerce were not particularly successful, after which I became a coach in a volleyball club and a secretary of that club, and that's where I still work today.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, you mentioned a moment ago that you were taking your exams when you received a summons from your unit. Do you recall approximately when it was that you received this summons from your unit?

utterances.speaker: MENDELJEV DJURIC
utterances.text: The exam that I passed on the -- 22nd June was followed by another exam on the 26th, which I missed because I was already gone then, so it must have been the end of June, between the 22nd and the 26th. I cannot tell you exactly which day.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: So what did you do in response to the summons, sir?

utterances.speaker: MENDELJEV DJURIC
utterances.text: It was the duty service that passed on to me the summons from Bijeljina, saying that I should report there. I went, and the duty service explained to me that I was to go to Mount Jahorina, to the newly-established training centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And, sir, just to be clear, did you actually report to Bijeljina, sir?

utterances.speaker: MENDELJEV DJURIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And was that the location of the command of the Special Police Brigade in June of 1995?

utterances.speaker: MENDELJEV DJURIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: When you reported to Bijeljina, were you told what your actual duties were going to be at the newly-established training centre in Mount Jahorina?

utterances.speaker: MENDELJEV DJURIC
utterances.text: No, nobody explained anything then, but I was told that Mr. Dusko Jevic was the director of that centre and that he will brief me.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And I take it you travelled to the centre, and if you would tell the Trial Chamber what happened when you arrived there.

utterances.speaker: MENDELJEV DJURIC
utterances.text: Upon my arrival at the centre, I noticed that it was based in Hotel Jahorina, which was a top-class hotel in that ski resort at Mount Jahorina, and refugee Serbs from Sarajevo had been put up there for a while, after which the hotel was in a rather bad condition, and then the training centre was placed there. When I met with Jevic, he explained briefly what was going on, that he had received orders to set up that centre. A number of recruits were already there. He told me what we were going to do with them, how we were going to train them, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Did you know Mr. Jevic prior to this, sir?

utterances.speaker: MENDELJEV DJURIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did. I've known him since elementary school. He was a few years ahead of me. And I know him also from my first days on the police force. I worked together with him then.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And did you also work together in the Special Police Brigade, performing these specialised tasks that you described for the Trial Chamber a few moments ago?

utterances.speaker: MENDELJEV DJURIC
utterances.text: Yes. We were together in this special brigade from the moment when it was established.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: If we could have some more identification, whether it is related to the period during war or before the war.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Thayer, you can address that.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I'm just getting to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Sir, can you put a date on when it first was that you and Mr. Jevic began working together in the Special Police Brigade?

utterances.speaker: MENDELJEV DJURIC
utterances.text: At that time, it was not a special brigade; it was a detachment for special assignments and missions, and it was from January 1982 [Realtime transcript read in error "1992"] until the conflict broke out in Bosnia, until the division and all other events that followed.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: A few moments ago, sir, you referred to some recruits that had been brought to the centre. Can you describe a little bit more who these recruits were?

utterances.speaker: MENDELJEV DJURIC
utterances.text: The information I received at the time indicated that these were people who had left the territory of Republika Srpska in different time periods, some right at the beginning of the war, some practically at the end, perhaps a couple of months before they were brought to the centre, and mostly these were people who left without the approval of Republika Srpska and happened to be able-bodied men.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lazarevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Just one small correction for the transcript. I believe I heard the witness saying that it was from January 1982. It's on page 73, line 4.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think the witness can address that himself. Do you agree with what has just been stated by Mr. Lazarevic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the gentleman please repeat his question?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Lazarevic wanted to know if it was 1982 or 1992, January 1982 or 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: When you first began to work with Mr. Jevic, sir?

utterances.speaker: MENDELJEV DJURIC
utterances.text: I started to work with Mr. Jevic before all of these events and before the formation of the Special Purpose Unit in January 1982.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you for that clarification. Now, when you were told by Mr. Jevic what was going on with the recruits, what were you told your specific assignment was going to be?

utterances.speaker: MENDELJEV DJURIC
utterances.text: The assignments were not given out specifically in terms of, "You will do this," or, "You will do that." We were simply a group of instructors who happened to be there, and our assignment was to train these people in basic military and police skills so that they can move in the field, how to move, how to find shelter, how to protect themselves, so that they would be in the position of coming into a combat zone and to be able to protect themselves and save themselves. It was just basic military training that was being conducted.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And were you assigned any command position?

utterances.speaker: MENDELJEV DJURIC
utterances.text: Yes, probably as one of the oldest and a person with the most experience, as I was appointed commander of the 1st Company.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And how many companies were there, sir?

utterances.speaker: MENDELJEV DJURIC
utterances.text: There were two companies.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And who was the commander of the 2nd Company?

utterances.speaker: MENDELJEV DJURIC
utterances.text: The commander of the 2nd company was Mr. Nedjo Ikonic.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And was Mr. Ikonic also an instructor at the training centre?

utterances.speaker: MENDELJEV DJURIC
utterances.text: Yes. I think so, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And did you know Mr. Ikonic prior to your assignment to the training centre?

utterances.speaker: MENDELJEV DJURIC
utterances.text: Yes, I knew all the instructors who were at the centre from before, because most of them, except for two of them, were members of this Special Purposes Unit before these events, before 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And do you recall the names of any of the other instructors who were serving with you at the centre?

utterances.speaker: MENDELJEV DJURIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Would you please share those names with the Trial Chamber?

utterances.speaker: MENDELJEV DJURIC
utterances.text: Ljuban Poprzen, Jevto Doder, Tomo Krstovic, Nedeljko Milidragovic. These are the names that I can recall of people who were there. There were two other persons from the police there whom I didn't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, sir, you're known by a nickname, is that correct, and if so, can you just tell the Trial Chamber what it is?

utterances.speaker: MENDELJEV DJURIC
utterances.text: From birth, my nickname has been "Mane" because of the length of my first name and because it's quite characteristic in our area, I was given the nickname "Mane."

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: So at this training centre, when you reported in July of 1995, who was your immediate superior?

utterances.speaker: MENDELJEV DJURIC
utterances.text: My immediate superior at the training centre was Mr. Dusko Jevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And to whom did Mr. Jevic report at that time?

utterances.speaker: MENDELJEV DJURIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jevic at that time frequently mentioned the assistant -- the assistant minister, Mr. Kovac, and since Mr. Jevic was a member of the Special Police Brigade, I really couldn't say which orders he received from the brigade and which orders he received from the assistant minister.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And at this time, do you recall who was the commander of the Special Police Brigade?

utterances.speaker: MENDELJEV DJURIC
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Goran Saric.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And did Mr. Saric have a deputy?

utterances.speaker: MENDELJEV DJURIC
utterances.text: Yes, his deputy was Mr. Ljubomir Borovcanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And by July of 1995, the Special Police Brigade had been organised into several detachments; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MENDELJEV DJURIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And do you recall just some of the names or areas from which these detachments operated or were based?

utterances.speaker: MENDELJEV DJURIC
utterances.text: Yes. There was a detachment in Sarajevo at the Ilidza. There was a detachment in Herzegovina. There was a detachment in Bijeljina. There was a detachment in Doboj. And later, two more detachments were formed in Prijedor, and after moving out from Sarajevo by the Serbian forces and the civilians, the detachment moved to Jahorina.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And, sir, in 1995, generally speaking, what types of assignments did these detachments carry out?

utterances.speaker: MENDELJEV DJURIC
utterances.text: The detachments were like independent units. That's where the name "detachment" comes from. They would cover a specific territory, but their activities were not limited to that territory, but depending on need, unit from the nearest area or several units would be engaged, depending on the assignment. We didn't have any kind of area of responsibility, but we worked as needed from task to task.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And did some of those tasks actually include combat, sir?

utterances.speaker: MENDELJEV DJURIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, I want to focus your attention to July of 1995 and to the VRS attack on the Srebrenica enclave. At some point in that period of time, sir, did you receive an order to take your company somewhere?

utterances.speaker: MENDELJEV DJURIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did receive an order to go to Bratunac.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And do you recall the date on which you received that order?

utterances.speaker: MENDELJEV DJURIC
utterances.text: I think the day before arriving. I got there on the 11th, so it was the day before I arrived. I'm not 100 per cent sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. And how was that order transmitted to you, sir? How was it communicated to you?

utterances.speaker: MENDELJEV DJURIC
utterances.text: The order was issued to me by Mr. Jevic, who told me that we had a police assignment in Bratunac and that we were going to Bratunac.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And have you ever seen a written copy of that order, sir?

utterances.speaker: MENDELJEV DJURIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: So please tell the Trial Chamber what you did in response to receiving that order from Mr. Jevic.

utterances.speaker: MENDELJEV DJURIC
utterances.text: On the 11th, I prepared the group of people, this company of mine. We went to Bratunac, and we arrived sometime in the afternoon. Mr. Jevic went to the Bratunac police station. After that, he came with one of the local policemen and explained that he would take us to the place where we would be billeted.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And do you recall what your accommodations were, sir, and generally where they were located?

utterances.speaker: MENDELJEV DJURIC
utterances.text: My unit, the one that I led?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MENDELJEV DJURIC
utterances.text: Yes. The local policemen took us up river along the Drina to a populated place. I don't remember the name of the village. I think it was a village. There was a school there. When we got there, there were many beds piled up there. I assume that somebody had stayed there before, and there was a kind of -- we made a kind of makeshift camp there using the beds in that school. It was five or six kilometres away from Bratunac, from what I can recall now.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Just the last question before the break, sir. Can you tell the Trial Chamber approximately how many men you had with you from the Jahorina Training Centre at this time?

utterances.speaker: MENDELJEV DJURIC
utterances.text: I don't remember the exact number of men. I didn't have any kind of diary or any documents that would help to refresh my memory. I think it was around 70, 70 men.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Thank you, sir, and I think that will do it for today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. We are adjourning now because our time is up. I need to advise you that between today and until when you finish your testimony, you're not to communicate with anyone or allow anyone to communicate with you to discuss or even mention the subject matter of your testimony. Is that clear?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We'll adjourn until tomorrow morning at 9.00. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: be reconvened on Wednesday, the 2nd day of May, 2007, at 9.00 a.m. 17 18 19 20 21 22 23 24 25
